inline_comments.comment: `bail()` silently terminates every active subscription by calling `listeners.clear()`. Consumers who called `onModuleGraphChange(cb)` receive an `unsubscribe` function that they reasonably expect to be the *only* thing that ends the subscription, but after any bail+restart cycle their handle becomes a no-op with no indication that the subscription is gone. An addon, for example, would register once and expect updates to continue across hot-reloads—instead it is silently dropped on the first bail. If subscriptions are intentionally scoped to a single server lifecycle, that contract should be documented in JSDoc on `onModuleGraphChange` and the returned `unsubscribe` function could be widened to reflect that. If subscriptions should survive restarts (which the returned `unsubscribe` handle implies), remove `listeners.clear()` from `bail()`: the new `watcherChangeHandler` created in the next `start()` call already routes through the same `listeners` Set, so survivors would be notified correctly without any extra work.

The `async` callback passed to `setInterval` returns a `Promise` that is neither awaited nor handled. If `server.waitForRequestsIdle()` rejects—for example because `bail()` closes the server during the `await` gap between `clearInterval(waitForModuleGraph)` on line 160 and the optional-chain call on line 163—the rejection becomes an unhandled Promise rejection and will trigger Node.js's `UnhandledPromiseRejection` warning (or abort in stricter environments). Per project conventions, all async operations that can reject must have explicit error handling. Wrap the body in `try { ... } catch { /* swallow or log */ }`, or refactor to a synchronous check pattern.

`buildModuleGraph` is exported as a top-level public symbol of `@storybook/builder-vite`, but it is a Vite-specific internal implementation detail that is not part of the `Builder<Config, BuilderStats>` interface. Exporting it solely to enable white-box unit tests creates an unintended API surface—downstream consumers could begin importing it and break on internal refactors. Consider either (a) moving it to its own internal module and importing it from there in tests, or (b) testing its observable behavior indirectly through the `onModuleGraphChange` callback to avoid exposing an implementation detail.

The `importers: Set<object>` and `importedModules: Set<object>` properties declared in `getOrCreateModuleNode`'s parameter type are never read inside the function body—only `file` and `type` are accessed. Listing them here adds noise, could mislead readers into thinking the function traverses them recursively, and will force callers that supply otherwise-compatible node-like objects to include these extra fields. Remove the two unused properties from the inline parameter type.

The variable named `debounce` holds a `ReturnType<typeof setTimeout>` (a timer ID), but the name strongly implies a debounce *function*. This makes it easy to confuse at a glance, especially alongside `clearTimeout(debounce)`. Rename it to `debounceTimer` or `changeDebounceTimer` to make the stored type immediately clear.

The `waitForModuleGraph` interval has no upper bound on the number of iterations. If the Vite server starts but never populates `fileToModulesMap` (e.g., an SSR-only project, an empty workspace, or a stalled initialization), this interval fires indefinitely at 1 Hz until `bail()` is eventually called from elsewhere. Add a maximum retry count (e.g., 30 attempts / 30 s), after which the interval self-clears and emits a `logger.warn` explaining that the initial module graph snapshot was skipped.

The `vi.mock('./vite-server', () => ({ createViteServer: vi.fn() }))` factory form is used here. Per `.cursor/rules/spy-mocking.mdc`, factory replacements should be reserved for modules that cannot be imported or must be entirely replaced. `./vite-server` is importable. The idiomatic form for this project is `vi.mock('./vite-server', { spy: true })` at the top level, with `vi.mocked(createViteServer).mockResolvedValue(fakeViteServer)` inside the existing `beforeEach`—which is exactly how the mock is configured on line 202.

The JSDoc comment says "Modeled after Vite's module graph" and explains the `Set<ModuleNode>` value semantics with "e.g. based on query params or import context"—both are Vite-specific implementation details embedded in a type that the PR describes as *builder-agnostic*. A future webpack5 builder implementing this interface would find the comment misleading. Revise the comment to describe the semantic invariant ("a single file path may resolve to multiple distinct module identities") without coupling the explanation to Vite internals.

general_comments.comment: The `onModuleGraphChange` function and the module-level `listeners` Set are both available before `start()` is called (subscriptions can be registered in any order), but there is no mechanism to deliver the *initial* module graph snapshot to a subscriber that registers after `start()` has already populated the graph. A late subscriber will see nothing until the next file-system event. Depending on how consumers are expected to use this API, it may be worth emitting the current snapshot immediately upon subscription when a server is already running (i.e., when `server` is already set and the graph is non-empty).

The five module-level mutable variables (`server`, `listeners`, `debounce`, `watcherChangeHandler`, `waitForModuleGraph`) make `index.ts` difficult to reason about in isolation and inherently break if more than one builder instance ever runs in the same Node.js module (e.g., in tests or a multi-server setup). The pre-existing `server` singleton establishes this pattern, but adding four more globals compounds the problem. Consider extracting the stateful pieces into a class or a factory function that returns a handle—this would also eliminate the need for `bail()` to clear `listeners` (each handle's `bail` would clean up only its own state) and resolve the subscription-lifecycle issue noted above.
